\paragraph{IRT and MFRM for LLM Evaluation.}
Item Response Theory (IRT) provides the psychometric foundation for principled ability estimation in LLM evaluation. \citet{jiao2025mfrm_llm} apply the Many-Facet Rasch Model to compare ten LLM raters with human experts, demonstrating that MFRM separates judge severity from examinee ability in this context, though their model includes no contamination term. PSN-IRT \citep{zhou2025psnirt} extends IRT to a neural four-parameter logistic framework that scales to large item pools but operates without judge or contamination facets. In educational measurement, \citet{uto2020generalized} show that generalized many-facet models with additional parameters remain identifiable under Hamiltonian Monte Carlo estimation, a result that supports the feasibility of G-MFRM's extended parameterization. The closest methodological antecedent is DG-IRT \citep{shu2013dgirt}, which uses binary gating to detect item preknowledge in educational testing. G-MFRM extends DG-IRT in three respects: continuous rather than binary exposure, explicit judge severity as a nuisance facet, and externally estimated exposure with formal identifiability guarantees (\S\ref{sec:identifiability}).

tool_args.old_string: We enforce non-negativity and sparsity of $c_n$ through a regularized horseshoe prior \citep{piironen2017horseshoe}. A global shrinkage scale $\tau_c \sim \text{HalfCauchy}(1.0)$ controls the overall contamination level, per-model local scales $\lambda_n \sim \text{HalfCauchy}(1.0)$ allow adaptive shrinkage, and a slab component $c^2_{\mathrm{slab}} \sim \text{InverseGamma}(2.0, 8.0)$ prevents unbounded estimates. The effective contamination is $c_n = |\tau_c \cdot \tilde{\lambda}_n \cdot c^{\mathrm{raw}}_n|$, where $\tilde{\lambda}_n$ is the regularized local scale. This prior strongly shrinks $c_n$ toward zero for clean models while permitting large values for genuinely contaminated ones, reflecting the expectation that contamination is sparse across the model population. The remaining priors are $\theta_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $b_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $d_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$, and standard uniform on thresholds $\tau_k$.
tool_args.new_string: We enforce non-negativity and sparsity of $c_n$ through a hierarchical HalfNormal prior. A global shrinkage scale $\sigma_c \sim \text{HalfNormal}(1.0)$ controls the overall contamination level, and per-model raw effects $c^{\mathrm{raw}}_n \sim \text{HalfNormal}(1.0)$ are scaled to obtain $c_n = c^{\mathrm{raw}}_n \cdot \sigma_c$. The HalfNormal support restricts $c_n \geq 0$, and the hierarchical structure provides adaptive shrinkage: when the data support low overall contamination, $\sigma_c$ contracts toward zero, pulling all $c_n$ values down. Models with genuine contamination retain large $c^{\mathrm{raw}}_n$ relative to the group. The remaining priors are $\theta_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $b_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $d_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.5)$, and standard uniform on thresholds $\tau_k$.
